newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: RTRS-RBA silence means no Feb policy move-analysts.
newsitem.headline: RTRS-RBA silence means no Feb policy move-analysts.

text.p: Australian financial markets remain on red alert for a cut in interest rates despite the silence of the Reserve Bank following its board meeting Tuesday.

The market is paranoid since being caught unawares by the last cut on December 11 which came a full week after the monthly meeting. But analysts say the silence is an emphatic signal a cut is off the agenda until the next meeting on March 4.
"The suspicions are misplaced," said Rory Robertson, a fixed income analyst at Bankers Trust. "If the RBA was going to cut in February it would have done so Wednesday."

"The market's wasting its time watching the screens," he added, referring to the daily ritual where dealers count down the seconds to 9.30 a.m. when the RBA updates its dealing intentions pages on Reuters and other news services.
Robertson said the central bank had a clear procedure for announcing policy changes agreed at a board meeting the day after and the late move in December had been an aberration.

"The bank fully intended to cut on December 4 but was frustrated by the tumble the dollar took the night before," he said. The local dollar had touched a six-year high of US$0.8212 on December 2 but collapsed to US$0.7855 offshore on December 3.

The savage selloff was partly triggered by comments from former RBA governor Bernie Fraser that he would have cut by a full point in November, unlike his replacement Ian Macfarlane who actually sanctioned a 0.5 point easing to 6.5 percent.
Robertson said the bank would have been reluctant to cut rates amid this turmoil, so held off for a week.
"But there were no exceptional circumstances this time which means the RBA believes the economy does not further stimulus at this time," he said.
Other analyts concurred and even thought the odds had lengthened on whether there would be another cut at all.

"Whilst the RBA could act in the next few days, we believe it is very unlikely and no action can be expected for the rest of February," said Bill Evans, general manager economic strategy and planning at Westpac Banking Corp.

Evans felt the RBA had been sufficiently encouraged by some early signs of a recovery in employment and building activity to hold off and allow the 150 basis points of easing already delivered to have its effect.
"A rate cut can only be expected for early March if the emerging upward trend in employment and building approvals was threatened by some very poor January data," he said.
Based on anecdotal evidence and a general view the economy had bottomed in the December quarter, he doubted the data would be weak enough to warrant such a move by the RBA.
Furthermore, he expected the economy to pick up strongly as 1997 progressed and saw growth runing at a speedy 4.75 percent in 1998, lessening the need for an easing.

"Consequently, we have changed our view that a rate cut can be expected in the first quarter and wwe now expect the RBA to leave rates unchanged for the remainder of 1997," Evans said. Westpac has consistently predicted another cut since the last move in December. -- Sydney Newsroom 61-2 9373 1800
